To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the distribution of the relative bibliometric indicator R2 = (citations)/(references) is lognormal with a standard deviation of around 1.3 and that the distribution of R1 = (citation)/(reference) − 1 is lognormal with standard deviation 2.1.

the distribution of the logarithm, ln, of a relative bibliometric indicator based on citation and references counts is approximately lognormal with a standard deviation of around 1.3 for publications with a citation count above 50, and that this distribution is independent of the publication year and of the field of research.

(a) the relative bibliometric indicators are universal and (b) they can be used for comparing publications from different disciplines or publication years, without the need for access to the world-wide citation graph
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new relative bibliometric indicator, the citation-reference index, and with the universality of this indicator, which is a prerequisite for the application of the indicator in the analysis of scientific performance.

the question: how can we measure the relative quality of scientific publications? Our results suggest that this can be done by comparing the citation and reference counts of individual publications with those of other publications in the same data set, and then taking the average of the logarithms of these ratios.
the universality of relative bibliometric indices and their use for comparisons of scientific publications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is evidence for universality of the relative performance of individual publications.
the relative bibliometric indicators are universal, and that they are independent of the citation count and the year of publication.

the universality of the distribution of relative bibliometric indices of individual papers is an empirical fact that can be exploited to compare publications across disciplines, publication dates and even different data sets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the logarithm of relative bibliometric indicators is a good measure of the quality of publications, regardless of discipline, year of publication or citation count.
the logarithm of a relative bibliometric indicator of the quality of a paper, such as its impact factor, is normally distributed.
the logarithms of relative citation and reference counts of scientific publications from a single source can be used as a proxy for a publication's scientific quality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of relative bibliometric indicators is independent of the citation count, and that it is well approximated by a lognormal distribution with a variance σ2 = 1.3.
the relative performance of individual publications can be compared across disciplines and across time, without having to know the absolute values of the citation counts.

the relative bibliometric indices we consider can be used to compare the relative quality of publications in different disciplines and publication years, and to compare the relative performance of different institutes or departments.
